entities.name: Assembly of Canonical Orthodox Bishops of France
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Assembly of Canonical Orthodox Bishops of France is the coordinating body for Eastern Orthodox Christian bishops in France whose dioceses are recognized as canonical (legitimate) by at least one autocephalous Orthodox church — bringing together bishops of Greek, Russian, Romanian, Serbian, Antiochian, and other Orthodox jurisdictions whose overlapping territorial presence in France represents one of the most complex canonical situations in contemporary Eastern Orthodoxy.

France has become one of the most jurisdictionally complex countries in Eastern Orthodoxy: unlike the traditional Eastern Orthodox practice of one bishop per territory (the principle of territorial episcopate), France has multiple Orthodox bishops of different national churches, all claiming canonical status, serving the same French territory. This situation arose from the 20th-century emigration waves — Russian emigration after the 1917 Revolution, Greek emigration throughout the 20th century, Romanian and Bulgarian emigration after WWII and communism, and various other waves — each bringing their respective national church structures.

The Assembly of Canonical Orthodox Bishops represents the ecumenical Orthodox effort to create coordination among these overlapping jurisdictions while working toward the long-term Orthodox goal of a single local church (according to ancient canonical principles). France's approximately 300,000-400,000 Orthodox Christians represent one of Western Europe's largest Orthodox communities, with the Russian Orthodox tradition (in its various subdivisions, including the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia, the Moscow Patriarchate Paris Diocese, and others) being particularly significant.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Assembly of Canonical Orthodox Bishops of France — coordinating multiple overlapping Orthodox jurisdictions created by 20th-century emigration, working toward canonical order in one of Western Europe's most complex Orthodox diaspora situations — is regionally significant as a monument to Orthodox ecumenical coordination.
